Digital preservation, as a domain of archival practice, presents distinctive challenges of format obsolescence, fixity verification, and long-term storage that have no precise analogue in the world of paper records. Emergent best practices are converging, though significant divergences across institutional contexts persist.

The description of archival holdings, traditionally rendered in finding aids whose structure mirrors the principle of provenance, has been complicated by user expectations shaped by the discoverability conventions of library catalogues and web search engines. The accommodation of these expectations without sacrificing archival principles is a continuing challenge.

It has been argued that traditional appraisal frameworks insufficiently account for records documenting the experiences of communities historically marginalised by mainstream archival institutions. Community archive movements have developed in response to this perceived deficit, with mixed implications for the broader archival enterprise.

Access policies in archives are shaped by a complex intersection of donor agreements, legal constraints, and professional ethical commitments. Tensions among these considerations are inevitable; their principled negotiation requires sustained engagement rather than mechanical application of fixed rules.

The archival turn in humanities scholarship has produced both productive engagements with archival materials and methodologically problematic ones. Closer collaboration between archival professionals and humanist scholars might productively address the latter without diminishing the former.

Records continuum theory, developed primarily within Australian archival scholarship, offers a framework for thinking about records that integrates creation, management, and use in ways that earlier life-cycle models did not. Its uptake outside its region of origin has been uneven.

Postcolonial critiques of archival practice have drawn attention to the ways in which collection priorities, descriptive vocabularies, and access protocols have reflected and reproduced colonial epistemic frameworks. The decolonial archive remains a contested project whose contours are still being articulated.

Recordkeeping in highly distributed digital environments raises questions about the stability of the record itself that earlier theoretical frameworks did not need to confront. The implications for evidentiary value, accountability, and historical reconstruction warrant sustained scholarly attention.

The empirical literature on present bias, while extensive, displays considerable methodological heterogeneity that complicates meta-analytic synthesis. Estimates of discount-rate parameters vary by an order of magnitude across studies, in ways not fully accounted for by sample or design characteristics.

Nudge interventions, despite considerable enthusiasm following their initial popularisation, have produced a more equivocal empirical record than early advocates anticipated. Recent meta-analyses suggest average effects that are positive but considerably more modest than the prominent individual studies had implied.

It has been argued that the canonical findings of behavioural economics have not transferred straightforwardly from the laboratory to field settings. The reasons for this attenuation are not fully understood and constitute an important agenda for ongoing research.

Loss aversion, considered a cornerstone of prospect theory, has been challenged by recent re-analyses suggesting that the empirical evidence for the phenomenon is weaker than commonly assumed. The debate remains active and bears on the proper scope of the theory.

The integration of behavioural insights into welfare analysis raises philosophical and methodological questions that have not been adequately resolved within the field. In particular, the choice of normative benchmark in the presence of context-dependent preferences remains contested.

Field experiments employing default-effect interventions have produced striking effects on outcomes including retirement savings participation, organ-donor registration, and consent to data sharing. Whether these effects reflect a unified underlying mechanism or distinct context-specific responses is unclear.

The replication record of canonical behavioural-economic findings, while better than that of some neighbouring fields, has not been entirely reassuring. Several prominent effects have failed to replicate at full original effect size, prompting reconsideration of theoretical claims that had come to be treated as established.

Bounded-rationality models, while heuristically appealing, have struggled to converge on a unified formal framework comparable in generality to expected-utility theory. The proliferation of competing approaches reflects both the difficulty of the problem and the absence of strong selection pressures from confronting decisive empirical tests.

It is sometimes claimed that behavioural economics has succeeded in displacing rational-choice models from the disciplinary mainstream. This characterisation considerably overstates the case; the dominant approach remains one in which deviations from rational choice are characterised relative to a maintained rational benchmark.

The translation of behavioural findings into policy recommendations has proceeded, in some cases, with insufficient attention to the conditions under which the laboratory or field findings were established. The resulting interventions sometimes underperform expectations in ways that retrospectively appear predictable.

The notion of equivalence, foundational to mid-twentieth-century translation theory, has been substantially destabilised by subsequent functionalist and descriptive approaches. The category nonetheless retains pedagogical utility, though its theoretical status is considerably more circumscribed than earlier accounts assumed.

Skopos theory, as articulated by Vermeer and elaborated by Reiß, locates the translator's primary obligation in the function the target text is intended to serve rather than in fidelity to source-text features. The framework has been criticised, with varying degrees of justice, for what some regard as an excessive instrumentalisation of translational practice.

Corpus-based approaches to translation studies have permitted the empirical investigation of features once accessible only through impressionistic observation. Findings concerning explicitation, simplification, and normalisation as putative translation universals have, however, attracted methodological scrutiny that has rendered their status considerably less secure than initially supposed.

It has been argued that the cultural turn in translation studies, while intellectually productive, has sometimes proceeded at the expense of sustained engagement with the linguistic and textual specifics of translated material. A more integrated approach would, in our view, serve the field better than the periodic oscillation between cultural and linguistic emphases.

The translator's visibility, foregrounded by Venuti and subsequent scholars, raises ethical and aesthetic questions that resist easy resolution. The polarity of foreignising and domesticating strategies, while heuristically useful, perhaps frames the issue more sharply than the actual range of translational practice warrants.

Retranslation, considered as a recurrent phenomenon in literary history, admits of explanations ranging from changing target-language norms to ideological shifts to the inherent inadequacy of any single rendering. The relative weight of these factors varies across cases in ways that have not been systematically theorised.

Machine translation, whose recent advances have transformed both the practice and the theory of translation, has reframed long-standing debates about translatability in ways whose full implications are still being absorbed. The relationship between human and machine translation appears unlikely to be one of simple replacement.

The sociology of translation, developed in the work of scholars including Wolf and Sapiro, attends to the institutional, economic, and prestige-related conditions under which translation is produced. The framework has illuminated features of the translational field that purely textual approaches could not have made visible.

Audiovisual translation, including subtitling and dubbing, raises distinctive theoretical and methodological questions that the dominant text-centred frameworks of the discipline have only partially addressed. The growth of the subfield reflects both intellectual interest and the increasing economic significance of the practices it studies.

The ethical dimensions of translation, including questions of voice, appropriation, and the politics of representation, have received increasing attention. The development of an adequate translation ethics — one neither reducible to professional codes nor floating free of practical constraints — remains an open project.
